entries.clue: Concerning discrimination that may be experienced following a meal (10)

annotation.definition: that may be experienced following a meal

blocks.note: after = concerning, as when you ask after someone
taste = discrimination, a fine sense of quality

annotation.surface: A remark about prejudice lingering once dinner is over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discrimination' reads as unfair treatment, but here it is the discerning kind: taste. 'Concerning' is the less familiar sense of AFTER, as in 'she asked after you'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the flavour that lingers in the mouth once you have eaten is the thing experienced after a meal.

entries.clue: It gets loaded in the morning moment (4)

blocks.note: mo = a moment, as in 'half a mo'

annotation.surface: Someone getting drunk first thing in the morning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' suggests drunk, but ammunition is what gets loaded into a gun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: ammunition is what you put into a gun when you load it.

entries.clue: In Paris, you twice assembled a short skirt (4)

indicatorNotes.In Paris: Paris is in France, so the word wanted is the one a Parisian would use
indicatorNotes.twice: twice means two times, so the same piece is written down two times

blocks.note: surface padding: the two pieces put side by side

annotation.surface: Someone in Paris putting together a skirt, apparently two times over.
annotation.walkthrough: TU is the familiar French 'you'; doubled, it gives the ballerina's skirt.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the tutu is the short, stiff, flared skirt worn by ballet dancers.

entries.clue: Sounding drunk, Ms Merkel’s not quite square? (11)

indicatorNotes.Sounding: sounding means making a noise, so the letters come from what the phrase sounds like when spoken

blocks.note: wrecked = drunk; Angela Merkel was the German chancellor

annotation.surface: A jibe that a tipsy Angela Merkel is a bit unconventional.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Square' suggests old-fashioned, but it is the shape: a rectangle is almost a square. The question mark admits the definition is playful.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful definition: a rectangle has a square's four right angles but not its equal sides, so it falls just short of square.

entries.clue: ‘Sentient’ tech runs alternative to stairs that’s used in an emergency (7)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition describes the answer as a thing used in emergencies rather than naming it

blocks.note: AI = artificial intelligence, tech that seems sentient
a lift is the British word for an elevator

annotation.surface: Talk of smart technology and an elevator you should use when there is an emergency.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sets up a fire notice about lifts, yet the answer is an emergency rescue by aircraft.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: moving people or supplies by aircraft is typically how disasters and evacuations are handled.

entries.clue: Buying and selling ingredients for jam? (7)

blocks.note: trade, often of an illicit kind, as in drugs or arms
not fruit and sugar: the cars and lorries that make up a road jam

annotation.surface: A market stall trading in the makings of preserves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jam' looks like fruit preserve; it is a traffic jam, whose ingredients are the vehicles.
annotation.definitionFit: Traffic is a plain synonym for trade, and the vehicles on a road are what a traffic jam is made of.

entries.clue: Best to have tricky situation reversed (4)

indicatorNotes.reversed: reversed means turned back to front, so the word is written from its last letter to its first

blocks.note: a spot = a tricky situation, as in 'a tight spot'

annotation.surface: Advice that the ideal is to turn a difficult situation around.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Best' is a verb here: to top someone is to beat them.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to best someone is to beat them, and so is to top them.

entries.clue: Cricketer’s futile redo botched … (10)

indicatorNotes.botched: botched means done badly, so the letters come out in a mess

annotation.surface: A cricketer's hopeless second attempt goes wrong, and the ellipsis runs on into the next clue.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': Cricketer is FUTILE REDO botched. The ellipsis links this to 8 down, whose sound-swap is about bowling.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: an outfielder is a cricketer stationed far from the bat.

entries.clue: … as polar bear is to dismiss a couple of batsmen? (10)

annotation.definition: … as polar bear is to dismiss a couple of batsmen?

blocks.note: the surface offers an Arctic animal; the setter wants its two opening sounds swapped over

blocks.clueFragment: to dismiss a couple of batsmen
blocks.note: in cricket, to bowl a batsman is to get him out, so this is 'bowl a pair' — the sound-swapped polar bear

annotation.surface: A cricket analogy: a polar bear stands to bowling out two batsmen as something else does.
annotation.walkthrough: Swap the first sounds of 'polar bear' and you get 'bowl a pair'. Following 7 down, where a botched futile redo is an anagram, this names the other word game at work.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a spoonerism swaps the initial sounds of words, exactly what turns polar bear into bowl a pair.

entries.clue: Tearing apart camel bone (10)

indicatorNotes.Tearing: tearing rips things into pieces, so the letters are ripped up and reassembled

annotation.surface: A gruesome scene of a camel being ripped to pieces.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tearing apart' reads as one phrase, but 'apart' is fodder and only 'Tearing' is the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the metacarpals are the five long bones in the palm of the hand.

entries.clue: Norman city’s best loved? Not entirely (2,2)

indicatorNotes.Not entirely: not entirely means only partly, so only part of the words is used

annotation.surface: Asking whether a town in Normandy is really the most popular.
annotation.walkthrough: Saint-Lô is a town in Normandy, France, badly damaged in 1944. The 's is 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Saint-Lô is the capital of the Manche department in Normandy.

entries.clue: Test consists of loud conflict, outcome of a duel (12)

blocks.note: is = consists of, as in 'the team is eleven players'

annotation.surface: An exam made up of noisy fighting, ending the way a duel does.
annotation.walkthrough: A gentleman insulted would demand satisfaction, which a duel provided.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical sense: satisfaction was the redress for an insult, and fighting a duel was how it was obtained.

entries.clue: In which money (by card) is blown? (5,6)

annotation.definition: In which money (by card) is blown?

indicatorNotes.blown: blown can mean blown apart, scattered by an explosion, so the letters are scattered

annotation.surface: A question about a day when people spend freely on cards.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blown' means spent recklessly in the surface and scattered in the wordplay, so the whole clue is both.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: Cyber Monday is the online shopping day after Black Friday, when money is spent by card.

entries.clue: Having a lot to offer? (10)

blocks.note: reads as having plenty; the setter means having a lot, an item numbered for sale
reads as having talents to give; the setter means putting that item up to bidders

annotation.surface: Praise for someone with plenty to give.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A lot to offer' sounds like many talents, but a lot is an item put up at an auction.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: an auctioneer offers lots, so selling at auction is literally having a lot to offer.

entries.clue: Swans: they have some brass (10)

blocks.note: a large North American swan species, named for its call
players who hold a brass instrument

annotation.surface: A claim that swans are wealthy, brass being slang for money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brass' is British slang for money, but here it is the instrument family: trumpeters play trumpets.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the trumpeter is a species of swan, and trumpeters are musicians holding brass instruments.

entries.clue: Joanna’s decent? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: the answer is a kind of Joanna, not a synonym for it

blocks.note: Joanna = piano in Cockney rhyming slang; this is the kind standing vertically

annotation.surface: A question about whether a woman called Joanna is respectable.
annotation.walkthrough: Joanna is Cockney rhyming slang for piano (said 'pianna'). The upright piano stands vertically, unlike a grand.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an upright is a type of piano, and an upright person is decent.

entries.clue: Fruit pie – the last – it’s his (7)

blocks.note: a baked fruit dish with a scone-like topping
a last is the foot-shaped block a shoemaker works on

annotation.surface: Someone claiming the final slice of pie for a particular man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The last' reads as the final piece, but a last is the shoemaker's form, and a cobbler mends shoes.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a cobbler is a baked fruit pudding, and a mender of shoes who works on a last.

entries.clue: One who hesitates verbally, missing intro; she takes a nosedive (7)

annotation.walkthrough: A tumbler is an acrobat, who dives and rolls on purpose.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: an acrobat who performs falls and rolls is one who takes nosedives.

entries.clue: All are reeling before end of stale beer (4,3)

indicatorNotes.end of: the end of a word is its final letter, so take the last letter of stale

annotation.surface: Drinkers all staggering after a stale pint.
annotation.walkthrough: Real ale is the British term for traditionally brewed, cask-conditioned beer.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: real ale is a kind of beer, conditioned in the cask it is served from.

entries.clue: Stuffy, with no issues, you say? (7)

indicatorNotes.you say: 'you say' points to speech, so the letters come from how the word is spoken

blocks.note: issue = offspring, so heirless means childless

annotation.walkthrough: 'Issues' reads as problems, but here it is offspring; with a silent H, heirless and airless sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a room lacking fresh air is stuffy.

entries.clue: Taking some chianti, besotted, somewhere on the Riviera (7)

annotation.surface: A drunken holiday on the Côte d'Azur, fuelled by Italian wine.
annotation.walkthrough: Antibes is a resort town on the French Riviera.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Antibes is one resort on the Riviera, between Nice and Cannes.

entries.clue: In Venice, orator rambling: it’s too much (12)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a phrase describing the answer rather than a noun

indicatorNotes.rambling: rambling means wandering aimlessly, so the letters wander out of order

annotation.definition: no one can walk away from here
